pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9, Using Weather Instruments (PROCEDURAL) — measure and record weather with a thermometer (°C), rain gauge (mm), wind vane (direction) and anemometer (speed), and keep a weather diary over time.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1/KS2 working scientifically — observe, measure and record; Y1 Seasonal changes (observe and describe weather); take and record measurements using standard units and simple equipment.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-ESS2-1 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]' (assessment limited to pictographs and bar graphs); builds on K-ESS2-1. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: pair each instrument with the quantity it measures and its unit; practise reading scales accurately (thermometer to the nearest °C, rain gauge in mm); record daily into a table and turn a week's data into a bar graph to reveal the pattern; emphasise consistent, fair measurement (same place/time).
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name three instruments and what each measures, read a thermometer in °C; Tier B — record several days into a table and build a bar graph; Tier C — read trends from the graph and use them to describe typical seasonal weather.
bestPractices: Match instrument → quantity → unit explicitly (thermometer/°C, rain gauge/mm, wind vane/direction, anemometer/speed)
Teach accurate scale-reading, especially eye-level thermometer reading and zeroing the rain gauge
Keep a real weather diary over at least a week so raw readings become a data table
Turn the table into a bar graph/pictograph (per 3-ESS2-1) so children see the pattern the numbers hide
Stress fair, consistent measurement — same location, same time of day — to make comparisons valid
keyRepresentations: An instrument panel pairing each tool with its quantity and unit
A weekly weather-diary table filling in day by day
A bar graph/pictograph built from the recorded data
A close-up scale (thermometer, rain gauge) for practising accurate reading
commonMisconceptions: A wind vane measures wind SPEED — it shows DIRECTION; the anemometer measures speed
The rain gauge shows total rain ever — it is read then emptied for each period
Reading a thermometer from an angle gives the true value — must read at eye level
Any single reading describes the weather — patterns need repeated, consistent measurements over time
Bigger numbers are always 'more weather' — units and what is measured matter (mm of rain vs °C)

learn.summary: Children aged 7–9 learn the procedure of measuring and recording weather: reading a thermometer (°C), a rain gauge (mm), a wind vane (direction) and an anemometer (speed), keeping a weather diary over at least a week, and turning the recorded table into a bar graph/pictograph so a pattern emerges. The core objective is a hands-on measure-and-record skill performed over time, with accurate scale-reading and consistent (same place, same time) measurement, culminating in the move from raw readings to a data representation.

activities.title: Weather-station logbook: read, record, graph
feedback: If the eye is not level with the liquid or the reading is rounded to the nearest large number, prompt: bring your eye level with the top of the liquid and read to the nearest marked line — and ask why that position matters (an angled line of sight misreads the scale, a parallax error).
For wind direction: the vane arrow points INTO the wind, toward where the wind is coming from, so name that direction — the one the arrow points to — not the way the wind is blowing toward.
For the rain gauge: read it on a flat surface at the meniscus, and empty it only AFTER you have recorded the value — otherwise you lose that reading.

If your gauge reads 0 mm even though you saw rain fall since your last reading, ask what could have gone wrong with the reading — was the gauge tilted, spilled, overflowing, or emptied before it was recorded?
If graph axis intervals are uneven or unlabelled: set equal intervals and label the axis with its unit before plotting.
Ask whether measuring at a different time of day would make the chart look different, and why — this is exactly why the time of day is kept the same each day.
When the week's bars appear, point to the shape: what do the tallest/shortest bars tell you about typical weather for these days?
activities.rationale: The objective is a procedural skill built by doing: reading real scales and logging values over time, then representing them. A growing diary table and an assembling bar graph rehearse both the measurement routine and the data-representation move. Interactive scale-reading with eye-level feedback, a value dropping into the table on each reading, and a graph that builds from the logged week are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are examples, not requirements.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]'; assessment is limited to pictographs and bar graphs.
DfE working-scientifically expectations include taking accurate measurements using standard units and simple equipment, and recording data in tables and simple graphs.
A wind vane indicates direction while an anemometer measures speed; consistent, repeated measurement is needed to reveal weather patterns.
learnerActions: Each 'day', read the thermometer to the nearest °C with your eye level with the top of the liquid, read the rain gauge in mm on a flat surface at the meniscus, note the direction the wind vane arrow points, and read the anemometer for wind speed (for example in km/h, or as spins counted in a set time on a homemade anemometer).
Write each reading into a weather-diary table with its date and unit (e.g. 12°C, 4 mm, wind from the west, wind speed 10 km/h or 15 spins in 30 seconds).
Repeat the routine for at least a week, keeping the place and time of day the same each day.
After a week, turn the table into a bar graph or pictograph with equal, labelled axis intervals, then read the pattern aloud (e.g. 'a run of cold wet days, then a warm dry spell').
Say why scientists measure consistently over time rather than relying on a single reading.
activities.intendedInsight: A single reading is real data, but it only shows one moment; a week of consistent, correctly-unit-ed readings becomes a data story, and a graph makes the pattern leap out of numbers that looked scattered — the step from measurement to representation.

activities.title: Match each instrument to its quantity and unit
feedback: If a learner says the wind vane measures speed, clarify: the vane shows direction (where the wind comes from); the anemometer measures how fast it blows.
If a learner compares numbers across quantities, remind them that mm of rain and °C of temperature measure different things and cannot be compared as 'more'.
activities.rationale: Establishing the instrument→quantity→unit mapping underpins the whole procedure and directly targets a common confusion (vane vs anemometer). A labelled diagram with tap-to-reveal 'what does this measure?' is one supporting scaffold; on its own it teaches the pairing but does not rehearse reading and recording, so it supports rather than replaces the logbook activity.
sourceClaims: A wind vane indicates direction while an anemometer measures speed; consistent, repeated measurement is needed to reveal weather patterns.
learnerActions: Pair each instrument with the quantity it measures and the unit used: thermometer → temperature → °C; rain gauge → rainfall → mm; wind vane → wind direction; anemometer → wind speed.
Explain in your own words why a wind vane does NOT measure speed and why the anemometer does.
Given a number with a unit (e.g. 15 mm, 15°C), say what was measured and why the unit matters — a bigger number is not simply 'more weather'.
activities.intendedInsight: Each instrument measures a specific quantity in a specific unit; knowing the pairing is the foundation for choosing the right tool and reading it correctly.

activities.title: Check the skill: read a scale and interpret a graph
feedback: For thermometer reading: confirm eye level and nearest-graduation reading; flag parallax errors (an angled view misreads the scale).
For graph interpretation: tie the answer back to the bars — the pattern is read off the data, not guessed.
For error-spotting: name the fix (level the gauge and read at the meniscus; the wind comes FROM the direction the vane arrow points; label the axis with its unit).
activities.rationale: A read-the-scale step and a graph-interpretation question check both parts of this procedure (measurement and representation) under observation; representing data to describe weather conditions links to 3-ESS2-1. Recognition-style questions confirm understanding but do not by themselves elicit the independent, repeated doing captured in the logbook activity.
sourceClaims: NGSS 3-ESS2-1: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]'; assessment is limited to pictographs and bar graphs.
learnerActions: Read a shown thermometer to the nearest °C, placing your eye level with the top of the liquid.

Given a completed weekly bar graph, answer questions about the pattern (e.g. which day was warmest, whether the week was mostly wet or dry, what the weather was usually like that week, and why more weeks of data would be needed to describe a whole season).
Spot and fix a problem reading: a tilted rain gauge, a wind direction reported backwards, or a graph with unlabelled axes.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct reading plus a correct interpretation of the graph shows the procedure has been learned, not just recognised.

constraints: This is a procedural skill: it is built by doing — reading real or realistic scales and recording values over time — so a version that only names or discusses instruments does not, on its own, rehearse the measuring and recording.

A labelled diagram or tap-to-reveal pairing is a useful scaffold for instrument→quantity→unit, but does not by itself give practice in reading and recording; pair it with actual measuring and logging.
Recognition or multiple-choice checks confirm the skill but do not elicit the independent, repeated measurement routine; keep an observed or hands-on 'do it over several days' component.
Measure consistently — same location, same time of day — so comparisons across days are valid.
Read the rain gauge then empty it; do not treat it as a running total of all rain ever fallen.
Read the thermometer at eye level to avoid parallax error, and read to the nearest marked graduation so rounding is consistent and kept small.
The wind vane arrow points INTO the wind, toward where the wind is coming from: name that direction (the one the arrow points to).
Observing the child perform the routine reveals procedural slips (parallax, backwards wind direction, mixed units, mis-scaled axes) that a verbal explanation would not surface.
Homemade instruments are acceptable; the point is accurate, consistent reading and recording.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three source claims are marked unverified in the original row (DfE working-scientifically and the Met Office/NOAA instrument claim); treat as legacy confidence, not re-checked.

Corrected a reversed/contradictory wind-vane instruction in the logbook feedback: the arrow points INTO the wind, toward the wind's source, so the direction the arrow points IS the direction the wind comes from — now stated consistently in every activity, constraint and the audit.

The original 'static image can't let the child practise' and 'dialogue can't deliver scale-reading' framings were softened: a diagram or discussion can support learning but does not by itself provide the repeated measuring/recording practice this procedural objective needs. This is a scope limit, not a claim that such media cannot teach.

The original '3D would add nothing / add cost without improving practice' claim was removed as catalog-ranking boilerplate not established by evidence; spatial depth is simply not central to reading scales and logging data.
The original diagnostic allowed a bar OR line graph; this guidance uses bar graph/pictograph to stay within the 3-ESS2-1 assessment limit, which is slightly narrower than the original wording.

probeDeeper: Show me exactly where your eye needs to be to read this thermometer — why there?
Your gauge reads the same as yesterday but the ground is wetter. What could have gone wrong with the reading?
If you'd measured at a different time of day, would your chart look different? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the thermometer at eye level to the correct scale in °C, reads the rain gauge on a level surface at the meniscus, reads wind direction from the vane correctly (the arrow points to where the wind comes FROM), records each with date and units, and transfers the log into a correctly-scaled, labelled graph.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the thermometer from an angle or rounds to the nearest big number (parallax and scale error)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model eye-level reading and reading to the nearest marked graduation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: eye not level with the liquid; misreads between graduations

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the wind as blowing TOWARDS where the vane points (vane direction reversed)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The vane arrow points INTO the wind — name the direction it comes FROM.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the rain gauge tilted, or empties/refills it between readings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read on a flat surface at the meniscus; empty only AFTER recording.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gauge not level, or resets it before recording

errorPatterns.pattern: Plots the graph with uneven or unlabelled axis intervals
errorPatterns.nextMove: Set equal intervals and label the axis with units before plotting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: axis spacing inconsistent; no units on the scale

responseLevels.gap: Cannot take a correct reading unaided — misreads scales, reports wind backwards, or records without units.
responseLevels.full: Independently takes accurate, correctly-unit-ed readings from all three instruments, logs them systematically, and produces a correctly-scaled, labelled graph — and could repeat the routine reliably on a new day.
responseLevels.partial: Reads each instrument correctly but is inconsistent in recording (missing units or dates) or mis-scales the graph.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a thermometer, a rain gauge and a wind vane (homemade versions are fine). Ask the child to take today's reading from each, record it on a simple chart with the date, and after several days turn the readings into a bar or line graph. Watch how they place and read each instrument and build the graph — don't ask them to explain the instruments, watch them use them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child DO it exposes procedural slips — parallax, misreading between graduations, reporting wind direction backwards, mixing up units, mis-scaling an axis — that a verbal 'how do you use a thermometer?' would never reveal.
